Canada has not stopped building homes. The bigger issue is that in many places, new housing has not been added fast enough to match population growth and household formation. When supply grows more slowly than demand, the result is usually higher prices, lower vacancy rates, and more competition for the homes that do exist.

Supply and demand in housing

Housing works like other markets in one important way: when many people want the same limited resource, the price tends to rise. But housing is different from many other goods because people need it to live, and they cannot easily wait for a better deal.

If a city adds only a small number of new homes while thousands of new residents, students, workers, and families arrive, the market becomes tighter. Even if some homes are being built, the shortage can still grow if demand rises faster than supply.

Simple idea: more demand + limited supply = more pressure on prices and rents.

What happens when supply falls behind

When there are not enough homes available, several effects usually appear at the same time:

  • Rents rise faster because tenants have fewer choices.
  • Home prices increase because more buyers compete for the same properties.
  • Vacancy rates fall, making it harder to find a place quickly.
  • Households delay moving, even when their current home no longer fits their needs.
  • People make compromises, such as living farther from work, accepting smaller units, or staying with relatives longer.

These effects are especially strong in fast-growing cities where land is limited, jobs are concentrated, and many people want to live near schools, transit, or family.

Why this is not just a construction problem

It is easy to think that housing affordability is only about builders putting up more units. In reality, the issue affects much more than construction alone.

Housing supply shapes:

  • Where people can live in relation to work, school, and services
  • How much income households must spend on shelter
  • Whether young adults can move out, rent independently, or buy their first home
  • Whether communities can attract and keep workers such as teachers, nurses, and service employees

When housing becomes too expensive, the effects can spread into the labour market, education, health care, and local business activity.

A closer look at the pressure on different households

Not everyone experiences a housing shortage in the same way. The effects depend on income, family size, location, and whether a household is renting or trying to buy.

  • Renters may face sudden rent increases, limited choices, and more frequent moves.
  • First-time buyers may find that saving for a down payment takes longer as prices rise faster than wages.
  • Families may stay in homes that are too small or move farther away from jobs and services.
  • Newcomers and students may struggle to find affordable units close to where they need to be.

Why the shortage can last for years

Housing takes time to plan, approve, finance, and build. That means supply cannot respond instantly when demand changes. Even if builders want to add more homes, delays in zoning, land assembly, labour availability, financing, and construction can slow the process.

Because of that delay, shortages can persist long after population growth has already changed the market. A city can be building more homes than it did before and still not be building enough to restore balance.

The main takeaway

Canada still builds homes, but in many places it does not build enough homes, fast enough, or in the right mix of types for the people who need them. That is why housing supply matters so much: it is a central driver of affordability, stability, and access to housing.

Understanding this relationship is the first step to understanding why housing has become harder to afford and why increasing supply is such an important part of the solution.
